reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents an easy Uniswap front-running bot tutorial that claims users can generate large or easy profits. It directs viewers to connect MetaMask, deploy external contract code, confirm wallet actions, send Ether to the contract, and fund it with about 0.5 to 1 ETH. The stated wallet profit-return arrangement is presented without independent verification of the contract behavior or financial outcome.

citations.quote: the front run smart contract bot that I recently developed that can help you make large amounts of profit within a short amount of time

The bot then places the buy order in the same block, which pumps the market slightly. The bot then waits for the identified transaction to come through, which executes at a higher price, and pumps the market even more.
Let's go to the wallet and send some funds to contract that we just created. I'm going to start with 1 Ether.
After it's sent to the contract and pressing the action button, then the bot automatically starts buying and selling for you give it some time to generate profit.
I usually leave it for about 24 hours and then I withdraw the profit.

opening.argument: The presentation includes a concrete risk qualification rather than an unconditional earnings promise. It warns that insufficient funding may cause gas and burn fees to exceed returns, identifies a maximum burn-fee condition, and recommends additional capital only to address that stated operational risk. That is materially different from presenting profit as certain. The speaker also describes a defined allocation model in which only part of the profit returns to the wallet, while the rest remains available for continued operation. These qualifications support treating the video as an operational explanation with financial uncertainty, not deceptive certification of a safe outcome.

citations.quote: I got messages from people who didn't fund the contract enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.
If you fund the contract with 0.4 ETH or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste in fees more than making a profit.
10% of profit automatically reenters the front-run pool, and automatically transacts back to your wallet 90% of the profit.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats profit-oriented language and funding instructions as proof of deception, but those facts do not erase the explicit warning that fees can exceed profits. Its claim that there is no independent verification is an evidentiary limitation, not proof that the creator knowingly misrepresented the tool. The quoted workflow establishes what the tutorial says the contract is intended to do, while the fee warning expressly preserves uncertainty about the result.

citations.quote: the contract will basically waste in fees more than making a profit.
give it some time to generate profit.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The fee discussion is a limited operational caveat, not a general warning that users may lose their deposited Ether or that the advertised mechanism may not work. The same description still says the contract automatically buys and sells at profit, while the narration calls the returns easy and reports a personal gain. A conditional warning about gas and burn fees does not substantiate the claimed trading outcome or make the funding solicitation non-deceptive.

citations.quote: immediately buy and sell at profit.
help you make large amounts of profit within a short amount of time
So I made around point three, Ethereum of profit.

opening.argument: The central activity is a programming and blockchain demonstration: creating a Solidity file, selecting a compiler version, deploying a contract through Remix, and observing the resulting contract interface. The speaker explains the intended transaction sequence and shows the software workflow rather than merely making a bare investment appeal. The supplied frames likewise depict development code, compiler controls, deployment controls, and blockchain explorer pages. On this record, the strongest characterization is an operational technology tutorial whose subject happens to involve trading, which fits an educational demonstration category.

citations.quote: create a new contract under contracts folder. We're going to name it BOT.
change the compiler version to 0.6.6 plus commit, plus 0.6c089d02.
So copy the address by clicking on the button, next to the generated contract address and head on over to EthanScan.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a tutorial is not a re-labeling of the evidence: the narration actually gives reproducible development steps, and the frames show the code and deployment environment. The prosecution's selected profit language describes the demonstrated use case, but does not establish that the educational format is a pretext or that the code performs as claimed. A technical demonstration can discuss expected results without becoming a verified financial offer.

citations.quote: So the following are the steps on how the Uniswap smart contract bot works.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The procedural format does not make the content merely educational when the procedure culminates in sending Ether to the deployed contract, activating it, waiting for profit, and withdrawing the result. The code and interface frames show implementation activity, but they do not prove the contract is safe, profitable, or capable of the promised front-running. The tutorial framing therefore does not answer the central financial solicitation.

citations.quote: I'm going to start with 1 Ether.
After it's sent to the contract and pressing the action button, then the bot automatically starts buying and selling for you give it some time to generate profit.

opening.argument: The material describes use of a software contract and its interfaces, not a downline, credential-harvesting, or membership scheme. The setup uses standard developer tools and wallet connection steps, and the stated interaction is with a deployed contract and its action function. The evidence does not establish that the creator requests a password, takes custody of a user's wallet credentials, recruits participants, or promises a guaranteed return. The presence of a funding step alone cannot prove a scam mechanism; it can also be an ordinary prerequisite for operating a blockchain-based tool, subject to the stated transaction and fee risks.

citations.quote: make sure you have MetaMask installed and connected to the Ethereum mainnet.
The remaining pool keeps front running for profit, until you transaction "Action" function in Remix
So go on over to Deploy and Run transactions and remix.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a deposit and a claimed return, but does not show that the creator receives the funds, guarantees repayment, or operates a recruitment structure. The instructions point viewers to a contract interaction and a public development environment, while the description acknowledges that fees can consume gains. Without evidence of a concealed transfer, credential request, or guaranteed outcome, the ordinary-tool interpretation remains plausible.

citations.quote: the transaction is confirmed, and our contract is funded.
anything lower but nowadays most of the tokens come with 3~6% fees.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam need not use recruitment or credential theft. Here, the creator directs viewers to deploy external code, send Ether into the contract, activate it, and wait for profit. The absence of a password request does not cure the financial risk, and describing the funds as a contract balance does not establish that users can recover them. The operational interface is precisely how the proposed return mechanism is presented.
